extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters, novelists, filmmakers, and storytellers planning story structure
extracted.subtask_short: writing a Save the Cat beat sheet
extracted.subtask_description: Create a beat sheet using Blake Snyder's 'Save the Cat' 15-beat template: list key plot beats across a three-act structure with approximate page timings to guide screenplay or story drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended beat count and page timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Different screenwriters have different opinions about how many, and which beats you should include in your beat sheet. There isn't one correct answer, but most people agree that you'll get good results from around 15 major beats spread across your story acts (as popularised by the Blake Snyder beat sheet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick note: The page numbers listed for each beat aren’t strict rules. They’re simply a guideline for where beats should roughly land in a 110-page screenplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 1. Opening image (p. 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of your opening beat is to immediately command the audience's attention. Your first visual should represent the struggle and tone of your story, giving a snapshot of your main character's problem before your screenplay starts in earnest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the opening scene of Rocky shows Rocky fighting inside an old church for $40, signalling his down-on-his-luck state and the film's theme. Your opening image should evoke an immediate emotional response that aligns with the protagonist's journey and foreshadow the character's arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 2. Set-up (pp. 1-10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present the status quo of the main character’s world, and describe their struggle or what’s missing. Establish where the story takes place, culture, people, timeframe, and give context before the overall story begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer where the story takes place, what the culture and people are like, and whether it's past/present/future. Plant seeds of change and introduce supporting cast (friends, family, mentors, antagonists). Ensure details are specific and intentional to set up contrast for upcoming change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 3. Theme stated (p. 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain what your story's about (often during the set-up). This theme is usually spoken to the main character or in their presence, though they may not understand it yet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give the audience the main character's name, a bit of their story, and defining traits. Weave the theme organically into the story so it acts as a lens for the character's actions and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 4. Catalyst / inciting incident (p. 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: A major event that jolts the status quo and propels the narrative into motion — the point of no return that engages the audience and forces change for the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: discovering a spouse is cheating, meeting someone who changes life, or other disruptive events. The catalyst separates the introduction from rising action and should hook audience curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 5. Debate (pp. 12-25)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the inciting incident, the protagonist doubts the journey ahead; this beat explores internal and external conflicts and tests the hero's resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this section to ratchet up tension by questioning the path forward, flesh out what's holding the character back, and deepen stakes. This beat makes the audience invested as the protagonist weighs whether to commit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 6. Break into Two (p. 25)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist makes a choice and their journey begins — a transition marking commitment to the new course of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On your beat sheet note why the protagonist chooses this path (searching for something, saving someone, internal vs external motivation). This pivot should flow from the inciting incident and debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 7. B story / subplot (p. 30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce the B story (often a love story) that discusses the theme and provides contrast or complement to the A story, exploring secondary relationships and perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the B story complements rather than overshadows the main plot, and that it weaves back into the A story by the end. The B story often provides timely advice or thematic insight that aids the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 8. Promise of the premise / Fun and games (pp. 30-55)
rubrics_metrics.description: The heart of the story where you deliver on the premise promised in the logline: set-piece scenes, action, laughs, and the central concept explored at its fullest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is where the audience gets what they came for — exploit the concept, show protagonist experiencing the new world, and include victories that build confidence (which likely won't last).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 9. Midpoint (p. 55)
rubrics_metrics.description: The halfway mark where things are either great or terrible for the protagonist: a false victory or rock bottom. Stakes are raised and the character's path is redefined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the midpoint to introduce a revelation or event that changes direction; re-evaluate pacing and ensure the character's transformation arc remains on track. It's a turning point showing character traits in high contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 10. Bad guys close in (pp. 55-75)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition tightens — villains, inner demons, or external pressures increase resistance, causing doubt, fear, and emotional exhaustion for the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document mounting obstacles leading toward the dark night of the soul. This beat ramps conflict so the middle of the story doesn't sag and emphasizes the protagonist's struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 11. All is lost (p. 75)
rubrics_metrics.description: A moment of apparent absolute defeat where something vital is lost or rendered meaningless — the 'dark night' precursor where the protagonist feels the goal is furthest away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the sense of loss palpable and personal to set up the emotional payoff. The audience should feel the weight of this low point; often something or someone 'dies' (literally or metaphorically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 12. Dark night of the soul (pp. 75-85)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist hits rock bottom and mourns what they've lost; everything seems to crumble before the new beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow the character to fully process defeat; this prepares them for the new discovery or idea that catalyzes the final act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 13. Break into Three (p. 85)
rubrics_metrics.description: With a new idea, discovery, or advice (often from the B story), the protagonist pulls themselves together and decides to try again — the internal transformation that pushes into the final act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This synthesis of lessons from the A and B stories should feel earned and lead to renewed, clearer motivation focused on the greater good rather than selfish aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 14. Finale (pp. 85-110)
rubrics_metrics.description: The resolution where internal and external conflicts converge and the protagonist's renewed effort leads to climax and consequence; narrative threads are resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the finale synthesizes the character's arc and theme so the moral of the story is clear and meaningful to the audience. Deliver satisfying payoffs to established stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 15. Final image (p. 110)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closing visual that should be the opposite of the opening image, representing the change the protagonist has undergone and leaving a lasting emotional impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about the lesson you want the audience to take away and how the final image encapsulates the character's arc and thematic resonance.
